fixes.explanation: David asks nothing about his own name here. The name he lifts up is God's, since he says God has exalted His name and His word above all else (Psalm 138:2). His final line is, "…do not abandon the works of Your hands." That's the request he makes, friend.
Sinai never shows up in these eight verses. David names exactly one direction, and it's toward God's holy temple. Nice try, friend, but that's a long walk to a spot this psalm never mentions.
David says the opposite. "On the day I called, You answered me…" No voicemail, no waiting room. He also says God emboldened him and strengthened his soul.

David says the kings will give thanks "…when they hear the words of Your mouth." The word is hear. I think that's a good moment for anybody, when somebody tells you good news and you can't stop talking about it.
Doubt isn't in the verse. David says the kings will give thanks "…when they hear the words of Your mouth." The word he uses is hear. Doubting would be a very different psalm.

David doesn't give the kings any orders in this psalm. He says they will sing "…for the glory of the LORD is great." The reason he gives is the LORD's glory, not anything David says. Nobody here is getting bossed around, friend. Not even the kings.

Armies? In THIS psalm? Not one. David says, "They will sing of the ways of the LORD, for the glory of the LORD is great." The reason he gives is the LORD's glory, and I'd be a fool to add a reason David didn't.
Fame doesn't come up in the verse. David says, "Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly…" The word he uses is lowly. Famous isn't in there, friend.
That's not what David says. The verse says, "but the proud He knows from afar." Nothing about lifting them up high in there, just that word afar.
The verse puts it differently. David says, "but the proud He knows from afar." Afar means at a distance, not sitting among them. I'd keep my seat at the table out of this one, friend.

David says, "If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me from the anger of my foes…" Notice the "if." He's picturing walking in the midst of trouble, not just around it. And he says God preserves him from the anger of his foes. I think that's a pretty comforting picture.
There's no sea and no storm in this psalm. David says God preserves him "…from the anger of my foes…" That's what the verse names, so a storm at sea isn't part of it.

David asks nothing about his own name here. The name he lifts up is God's, since he says God has exalted His name and His word above all else (Psalm 138:2). His final line is, "…do not abandon the works of Your hands." That's the request he makes, friend.
